definition: The full range of electromagnetic waves, ordered by wavelength (or frequency or photon energy), from radio waves to gamma rays. All of it travels at c and is made of photons.
The longest-wavelength EM waves (roughly 30 cm and longer). Made and detected by oscillating currents in antennas; photon energies far too small to affect atoms.
EM waves from about 1 mm to 30 cm. Used for Wi-Fi, radar and microwave ovens; they can set polar molecules such as water rotating.
EM waves from about 700 nm to 1 mm. Emitted strongly by objects at everyday temperatures and absorbed by molecular vibrations.
The narrow band from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red), photon energies about 1.8 to 3.1 eV, that human eyes detect.
EM waves from about 10 nm to 400 nm. Energetic enough to break chemical bonds (sunburn); the shortest UV can ionize atoms.
EM waves from about 0.01 nm to 10 nm, photon energies of roughly 100 eV to 100 keV. Pass through soft tissue and diffract from crystal planes.
The highest-energy photons, usually defined by their origin in atomic nuclei (radioactive decay, nuclear reactions) rather than by a strict wavelength cutoff.
A band of wavelengths that the atmosphere lets through to the ground, chiefly visible/near-infrared light and radio waves.
EM radiation whose photons carry too little energy (below roughly 10 eV) to knock electrons out of atoms: radio, microwave, infrared, visible and most UV.
